eoce-003.title: Oxygen in the air roughly doubles
eoce-003.text: At about the start of the Eocene, roughly 56 million years ago, the air itself changed. The amount of oxygen in Earth's atmosphere more or less doubled. Every breath taken by an early Eocene animal held far more oxygen than the air of only a short while before. The shift came just as the new, hot epoch began.

eoce-011.title: Modern mammal orders burst onto the scene
eoce-011.text: Most of the major branches of today's mammals show up in the rocks almost at once. The warming of {{ref:pale-048}} brought more modern mammal groups into North America while many Paleocene forms declined. The oldest fossils of most modern mammal orders appear within a brief early Eocene window. Among them are artiodactyls, the even-toed hoofed mammals, and perissodactyls, the odd-toed ones. Hyaenodontids, meat-eaters, arrived too. The odd-toed ungulates seem to have arisen in Asia: Cambaytherium, from western India, dates to roughly 54.5 million years ago. The newcomers shared a new body plan. They had long thin legs, grasping hands and feet, and teeth shaped for chewing. All were small, under 10 kg. In fact, Eocene mammals were only about 60% the size of the Paleocene mammals before them.

eoce-009.title: The Fur Formation, a Danish fossil treasure
eoce-009.text: Northern Denmark keeps a layered diary of the earliest Eocene. About 60 m of diatom-rich clay, with up to 180 ash layers, settled on the earliest Eocene seafloor there. Diatoms are single-celled algae with glassy shells. Laid down just after the PETM, the deposit holds a tropical to subtropical flora that points to a climate about 4–8 °C warmer than today. It preserves abundant fish, insects, reptiles, birds and plants, including one of the richest Eocene fossil insect faunas.

eoce-004.title: Champsosaurs, the last crocodile look-alikes, die out
eoce-004.text: Champsosaurus survived the asteroid that killed the dinosaurs, but not the heat that followed. It and its crocodile-like relatives, the neochoristoderes, died out in the early Eocene. Their loss coincides with the turnover of mammals linked to the warmth of the PETM. Only the small lizard-like Lazarussuchus carried the wider choristodere line on, in Europe, until the Miocene.

eoce-010.title: Gastornis, the giant flightless bird
eoce-010.text: In the forests of the early Eocene stalked a bird too big to fly. Gastornis, a large flightless bird, appears in the fossil record about 56 million years ago. It lasted a long time, going extinct only about 40 million years ago. Birds, not just mammals, produced giants after the dinosaurs.

eoce-014.title: The first true primates
eoce-014.text: The oldest ancestor of every monkey, ape and human known so far was a tiny animal called Archicebus achilles. It lived about 55 million years ago, and it is the earliest known ancestor of primates. At the start of the Eocene, true primates spread fast. In North America, tarsier-like omomyids and lemur-like strepsirrhines replaced the archaic plesiadapiforms of {{ref:pale-018}}. Primates moved between North America and Asia around 55.8 million years ago, across the land links of the time. Then the family tree branched. Primates split into strepsirrhines, the lemurs and lorises, and haplorhines, the tarsiers and anthropoids. The anthropoids are the branch that would one day include monkeys, apes and people. By about 50 million years ago, both branches had diversified.

eoce-017.title: Songbirds, parrots and loons appear
eoce-017.text: Many of the birds at a backyard feeder belong to orders born in the Eocene. Songbirds, parrots, loons, swifts and woodpeckers all first appeared then. The oldest known stem loon, Nasidytes, comes from England's London Clay, about 55 million years old. The first perching birds, the passerines, appear around 52.5 million years ago. The woodpecker order dates from the early Eocene, and the kingfisher order from the middle Eocene.

eoce-015.title: India hits Asia and the Himalayas begin to rise
eoce-015.text: The world's highest mountains are the crumple zone of a continental crash. India's collision with the Eurasian plate is most often dated to about 55–50 million years ago, though the exact timing is debated. India's northwestern corner touched Eurasia first, about 55 million years ago. Contact along the Yarlung–Zangbo suture, the seam where the two plates join, began around 50 million years ago. The impact shows in India's speed. Around 55 million years ago its plate slowed from about 18–19.5 cm a year to about 4.5 cm a year, circumstantial evidence of the collision. The crash closed the Tethys Ocean there and began thrusting up the Himalayas and the Tibetan Plateau. Not everyone accepts this picture. Rival models have a microcontinent colliding first, with India itself arriving only around 40 million years ago, or even at the end of the Oligocene. The timing and nature of the collision remain genuinely contested.

eoce-016.title: The Pyrenees take shape
eoce-016.text: The mountains between Spain and France were built by a long, hard squeeze. Iberia and Europe, converging since about 100 million years ago, collided in the Eocene and Oligocene. From about 55 million years ago the Pyrenees underwent very strong crustal compression, which set up the range's present structure. This main phase lasted until about 47 million years ago. It shortened the crust by about 4 mm a year and stacked sheets of rock one on top of another.

eoce-021.title: The North Atlantic splits Greenland from Europe
eoce-021.text: The old northern supercontinent Laurasia finally broke in two when the North Atlantic opened. By 56 million years ago Greenland was already its own plate, cut off from North America by the Labrador Sea–Baffin Bay rift. Seafloor spreading then crept north from the Labrador Sea and Baffin Bay. By about 54 million years ago, it had split Greenland from Eurasia. The break-up volcanism of {{ref:pale-030}} ran from about 56 to 54 million years ago, forming the Iceland Plateau and Greenland's Skaergaard intrusion. Extension between North America and Eurasia also opened the Eurasian Basin across the Arctic.

eoce-020.title: The London Clay's tropical flora
eoce-020.text: Under the streets of London lie the fruits of a tropical forest. Shallow seas over southeast England laid down the London Clay, rich in fossil seeds and fruits of some 350 plant species. Its flora includes tropical plants that now grow in Asia. They are a sign of how much warmer the early Eocene climate was.

eoce-018.title: The Early Eocene Climatic Optimum
eoce-018.text: Alligators once lived north of the Arctic Circle, and palms grew in Alaska. That was the world of the Early Eocene Climatic Optimum, the EECO. It was a long spell of extreme greenhouse warmth, the warmest sustained interval of the whole Cenozoic. A series of intense early Eocene hyperthermals set it off, including {{ref:eoce-022}} and {{ref:eoce-025}}. Global mean surface temperature is estimated at about 23–30 °C. The hothouse from 56 to 47 million years ago ran about 14 °C warmer than today. Antarctic summers reached about 25 °C. Amphibians, too, lived in the Arctic. The warmth puzzles scientists. Climate models struggle to reproduce such warm poles and mild polar winters, a puzzle called the equable climate problem.

eoce-022.title: Eocene Thermal Maximum 2, nicknamed Elmo
eoce-022.text: After the PETM, the Earth ran a second, smaller fever. ETM-2, also called H-1 or Elmo, was a brief burst of global warming, the second major hyperthermal after {{ref:pale-048}}. It left a smaller drop in carbon-13 and was less severe. Its timing is strikingly regular: it came exactly 4.5 long orbital-eccentricity cycles after the PETM. Eccentricity is how stretched Earth's orbit is, and it changes on a slow rhythm. That pattern suggests orbital forcing may have triggered it. Smaller hyperthermals followed within about a million years, and together they led into the warmest part of the Eocene.

eoce-023.title: The Green River lakes
eoce-023.text: Some of the world's most beautiful fossil fish come from lakes in the Rockies. Mountain building there created basins where Lakes Gosiute, Uinta and Fossil Lake laid down the oil shales of the Green River Formation. Their bottom muds held little oxygen. That slowed decay and kept scavengers away, preserving fish, leaves and even soft parts of insects. The formation is perhaps the best record of Cenozoic freshwater life, with fish, crocodilians, birds and mammals. The climate was frost-free, so crocodiles lived among sycamore forests, even as the moist early Eocene turned slightly drier.

eoce-024.title: Pakicetids, the first whales, walked on land
eoce-024.text: The first whales had hooves. The pakicetids, a family of hoofed land mammals that lived about 53 million years ago, are the earliest whales. Their closest known relative was Indohyus, of the family Raoellidae. Even on land, pakicetids already had a whale's ear: they could hear under water through bone conduction rather than eardrums. Bone conduction carries sound through the skull bones themselves. It was the first step on a remarkable journey. During the Eocene, whales became very diverse and made the full transition from land to sea. That path runs through {{ref:eoce-036}} to the giant, fully marine {{ref:eoce-061}}.

eoce-025.title: Eocene Thermal Maximum 3
eoce-025.text: Hothouse worlds tend to come in a sequence of spikes. ETM-3, informally the K or X event, was another early Eocene hyperthermal, about 52.8 million years ago. It is marked by a pulse of isotopically light carbon, the kind released from organic matter. Its carbon-isotope excursion marks the onset of {{ref:eoce-018}}.

eoce-027.title: Eohippus and the first horses
eoce-027.text: The ancestors of horses were small forest animals. The first equids lived in North America by the earliest Eocene, with early relatives of unclear affinity in Europe. Eohippus appeared about 52 million years ago. One of its species branched into various new types of horse. Thousands of complete skeletons come from Eocene layers, mainly in Wyoming's Wind River basin. About 50 million years ago Eohippus graded into Orohippus. That gave rise to Epihippus, with better grinding teeth, about 47 million years ago. Their European cousins, the palaeotheres, arose later in the early Eocene.

eoce-028.title: The first bats take to the air
eoce-028.text: Only about 16 million years after the dinosaurs died out, mammals learned to fly. The earliest known bats, such as Onychonycteris, appear about 52 million years ago. With bats, mammals had colonized the air by the Eocene. Bats also travelled far: lineages crossed from Africa to South America during the Eocene, possibly by way of Antarctica.

eoce-026.title: Cambay amber, an Indian insect trap
eoce-026.text: Tree resin is a perfect trap for small creatures, and it can hold them for tens of millions of years. Amber from Gujarat, India, preserves an important early Eocene assemblage of arthropods, mostly insects. It dates to about 52–50 million years ago, around the time India was meeting Asia.

eoce-029.title: The Okanagan Highlands lakes
eoce-029.text: Even the mountains of the Pacific Northwest grew palms in the Eocene. Lakes in the uplands of British Columbia and Washington preserved detailed plants, insects and fish through {{ref:eoce-018}}. Fossil palm beetles at McAbee, dated to about 52.9 million years, show that palms grew there. The 48.7-million-year-old Princeton Chert preserves plants in anatomical detail. It also holds the oldest known ectomycorrhizal fungi, which wrap around tree roots and trade nutrients with them.

eoce-032.title: Cats and dogs part ways
eoce-032.text: The split between cat people and dog people goes back about 50 million years. The ancestors of cats and of dogs diverged then, among the first true carnivorans. Arctoids, the branch of bears, weasels and raccoons, are known on all continents from 46 million years ago. Early carnivorans stayed small, while oxyaenids and mesonychians held the top-predator roles. Crown-group carnivorans, the branch that includes all living members, first appeared around 42 million years ago.

eoce-035.title: The Sevier orogeny ends
eoce-035.text: A belt of thrust faults in western North America had been folding and stacking rock for a very long time. Deformation in the Sevier fold-and-thrust belt, under way since about 160 million years ago, ended around 50 million years ago. In southwestern Utah, some Sevier thrusts may have stayed active until later in the Eocene.

eoce-034.title: Monte Bolca, the fishbowl of Verona
eoce-034.text: Some fossil fish from Italy still show their colors. Near Verona, low-oxygen mud preserved fish so well that their organs are often intact, and skin color can sometimes be read. The site's Pesciara, meaning 'fishbowl', is famous for these extraordinarily well-preserved Eocene fish, from about 50–49 million years ago.

eoce-036.title: Ambulocetus, the walking whale
eoce-036.text: About 49 million years ago, whales were part crocodile in style. Ambulocetus was a probably amphibious early whale that lived, crocodile-like, in the bays and estuaries of the Tethys Ocean, in what is now northern Pakistan. By then, whales had returned to the water. Ambulocetus marks the halfway point between {{ref:eoce-024}} and fully marine whales.

eoce-037.title: The great Eocene cooling begins
eoce-037.text: About 49 million years ago, the planet's thermostat turned, and a long cooling began. The warming climate gave way to cooling, a slow trend that lasted until about 34 million years ago. Changing geography drove the first drop. As Australia and South America drew away from Antarctica, ocean circulation shifted. Falling carbon dioxide kept the cooling going. It was drawn down by organic productivity and by the weathering of new mountains. Models suggest the carbon dioxide mattered more than the isolation of Antarctica's ocean. Signs of cold appeared. Cold-water diatoms suggest winter sea ice formed in the Arctic, and Antarctica shows glaciation by about 37 million years ago. The cooling that began in the middle Eocene ultimately led to the ice ages of the Quaternary.

eoce-038.title: The Azolla event: a fern that cooled the world
eoce-038.text: A tiny floating fern may have helped pull Earth out of its hothouse. In the middle Eocene the Arctic Ocean was almost cut off from the wider seas. Its warm surface and high carbon dioxide let the fern Azolla grow rapidly across it. With modest warmth and 20 hours of polar summer daylight, Azolla can double its mass in two to three days. When the ferns died, they sank to the stagnant seafloor. Over about 800,000 years, they were buried in sediment, building large deposits that locked away carbon. Carbon dioxide fell catastrophically, from about 3,500 ppm in the early Eocene to 650 ppm during the event. The drawdown is believed to have ended the early Eocene warmth about 48.5 million years ago. Temperatures fell rapidly from 49 to 47 million years ago. Soon glacial dropstones, rocks carried out by floating ice, became common in Arctic sediments.

eoce-041.title: Lutetian limestone, the stone of Paris
eoce-041.text: The Louvre is built from the floor of an Eocene sea. In the middle Lutetian, a sea over the Paris Basin laid down marine limestone, later topped by freshwater limestone and marl once the sea withdrew. The Lutetian age, 48.07–41.03 million years ago, is named after this stone, from Lutetia, the ancient name of Paris. Used since Roman times, this 'Paris stone' built many of the city's grandest buildings, including parts of the Louvre and the Arc de Triomphe.

eoce-039.title: Rifts open across western Europe
eoce-039.text: The same collision that raised the Alps also tore western Europe open. From the Eocene onward, the ongoing Alpine collision opened a north–south system of rifts, long valleys where the crust pulls apart. The Limagne Graben formed in the middle Eocene and held a lake. Rifting also began in the Bresse Graben.

eoce-040.title: Grasses spread and the first savannas appear
eoce-040.text: Grasslands began as a thin fringe along rivers. As the climate cooled and dried after the EECO, grasses began to spread. During the Eocene they moved out from riverbanks into open tracts. Subhumid savannas, open grassy country with scattered trees, are known in South America from the middle Eocene. The change opened new country for grazing animals.

eoce-044.title: The Kula plate disappears beneath Alaska
eoce-044.text: An entire tectonic plate can be swallowed whole. The Kula plate had been subducting under Alaska and the Yukon since the early Eocene. Around 48 million years ago it was entirely consumed. Only a slab of it remains, deep in the mantle under the Bering Sea.

eoce-043.title: Geiseltal, a German lignite treasure
eoce-043.text: A coal mine in central Germany turned out to be a vault of Eocene life. A coastal moorland of lakes and tidal bays there preserved over 50,000 fossil vertebrates, along with insects and plants. Its soft tissues were among the very first found from the Eocene. Its mammals are so characteristic that they define a European land-mammal stage.

eoce-045.title: Forests near the poles
eoce-045.text: Some of the strangest Eocene forests grew where today there is only ice and tundra. High-Arctic river deposits in Nunavut preserve old-growth conifer forests where they stood, with leaf litter preserved down to the molecular level. Swamp cypress and dawn redwood grew on Ellesmere Island, and subtropical plants in Greenland and Alaska. In the far south, pollen from Prydz Bay shows taiga forest grew in Antarctica too.

eoce-047.title: The Messel Pit
eoce-047.text: In a German pit, fossils still show fur, feathers and the outlines of skin. About 47 million years ago a lake at Messel, in Hesse, Germany, preserved over 1,400 kinds of plants and animals, the best record of its time. It was a maar lake, a deep crater lake left by a volcanic blast, ringed by lush subtropical forest. The climate was close to {{ref:eoce-018}}, with a mean yearly temperature of 22 °C, and the site lay 10° farther south. Animals sank into deep, oxygen-poor water where no scavengers reached them, so whole skeletons survive. How they died is debated. Bursts of toxic volcanic gas, like Lake Nyos in 1986, may have killed them; others blame toxic cyanobacterial blooms. Its fossils, from pygmy horses and early primates to bats, keep yielding major discoveries about early mammals and birds.
